title: USCIS May Stop Deferring to Prior Approvals Under Visa Extension Proposal
excerpt: DHS proposes deleting the rule that tells officers to follow an earlier I-129 approval on extensions for the same worker and job. Comments close November 13; the current rule stays in force until a final rule is published.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed ending the rule that directs USCIS officers to defer to a prior approval when the same employer seeks an extension for the same worker in the same job.
  • The proposal, published October 14, would delete 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) and covers Form I-129 extensions, including H-1B, L-1 and O-1 petitions; DHS estimates it would affect about 208,429 petitions a year, according to reporting of the proposal.
  • Public comments close today, November 13, 2026. Nothing changes yet: the deference rule stays in force unless DHS publishes a final rule.
  • If your extension is coming up, build the filing as if it were a first petition — document current duties, the wage actually paid, payroll records and the worker's qualifications.

Employers extending an H-1B, L-1 or O-1 worker's stay have long relied on a simple protection: if USCIS approved the petition before, and nothing material has changed, the officer reviewing the extension should generally follow that earlier decision. The Department of Homeland Security now proposes to remove that protection. Its notice of proposed rulemaking, Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility (91 FR 65119), published on October 14, would delete the regulation at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) that directs officers to defer to a prior Form I-129 approval unless there was a material error, a material change, or new information undermining eligibility.

Who is affected, exactly

The proposal concerns Form I-129 extension petitions — the route used for H-1B, L-1 and O-1 workers, with reporting on the proposal also naming TN and E categories. It does not change initial petitions, green card filings, or work permits. DHS estimates the change would affect around 208,429 petitions each year, according to reporting of the proposal by The Times of India, citing figures shared by immigration law firm Reddy Neumann Brown. For the Indian diaspora, the exposure is concentrated in H-1B extensions: Indian nationals receive the large majority of H-1B approvals, and most long-serving tech workers pass through several extensions on the road to a green card.

What would change in practice

Deference is the mechanism that keeps an extension from becoming a fresh adjudication of a job USCIS already approved. Under the current rule, an officer gives weight to the earlier approval when the parties and the underlying facts are the same. Under the proposal, officers could still consider an earlier approval but would no longer be required to follow it — each extension could be examined as though the underlying eligibility question were open again. The practical risk employers cite is more requests for evidence and more denials on facts that were settled years earlier. A detailed breakdown of the proposal and its place in this autumn's rulemaking is in Gozel Law's November 2026 immigration bulletin.

A rule that has reversed before

The deference policy has changed direction repeatedly. USCIS first adopted it in a 2004 memorandum, rescinded it in October 2017, restored it in the Policy Manual in April 2021, and wrote it into the regulations in December 2024. The October proposal would reverse the 2024 codification. Because this is a notice of proposed rulemaking rather than a final rule, the existing regulation remains in effect today, and DHS must consider public comments before any final version takes effect.

What to do now

Comments on the proposal are due today, November 13, 2026, in Regulations.gov docket USCIS-2026-0529; employers whose extensions were spared repeat evidence requests by deference are the commenters DHS expects to hear from. For workers with an extension in the next year, no filing rule has changed — but immigration counsel advising on the proposal suggest preparing each extension as a first filing: current job duties as they stand today, the wage actually paid, payroll records, and full qualification evidence. H-1B extensions can generally be filed up to six months before the requested start date, and how a final rule would treat petitions already pending is not yet known, which makes the timing of upcoming extensions worth a conversation with counsel now rather than after a final rule lands.
